headline: Moody's warns Australian bank earnings face headwinds from housing slowdown and lower credit growth
reasoning: Daniel Yu of Moody's Ratings argues that weaker housing conditions will reduce housing turnover, causing banks to write fewer home loans — which are approximately 60% of total bank loan books. Lower credit volumes will weigh on earnings even if rates remain elevated. A shift in loan mix away from investor loans (historically ~41% of home lending) toward owner-occupier loans will also compress margins, since investor loans carry higher interest rates. Additionally, softer GDP growth (forecast cut to 1.9% for 2025 and 1.6% for 2026) and higher rates will push up non-performing loans and require larger provisioning, as already seen in NAB and Westpac's first-half 2026 results.
quote: So weaker housing conditions means lower housing turnover at least in the short term. As you know, we think buyers will probably hold off as they want to see how much further prices may fall. And that means with less buyers, sellers may also start to postpone their their plans to sell until more buyers start to return to the market. So with lower turnover housing turnover, that means the banks are writing less home loans, which is a key driver to their earnings, because at a system level, home loans make up about 60% of total bank loans.
episode_title: Moody's sees housing slowdown weighing on bank earnings

headline: Moody's sees marginal asset quality benefit for Australian banks if investor loan share declines, but historical performance gap is small
reasoning: Daniel Yu from Moody's notes that investor loans make up around 41% of total home lending volumes in Australia. Investor loans are structurally riskier than owner-occupied loans — they are typically written at higher LVRs, are often interest-only, and attract higher interest rates from banks to reflect the added risk. If the investor share of the mortgage book declines structurally, Yu argues there could be a marginal positive for bank asset quality. However, he cautions that historically the performance of investor loans has been pretty similar to owner-occupied loans, so the benefit to asset quality would likely be marginal rather than material.
quote: if you look at the historical performance of investor loan, it's been pretty similar to its own occupied. So I think the benefit to asset quality as, as you get less investors is probably going to be marginal. Investor loans, you know, typically have taken up about 41% of total home lending volumes. If that does decline, I think there are some marginal benefits because the characteristics of an investor loan is slightly riskier than an occupied. So if you think about the typical investor loan, it's done at a higher LVR. It's typically interest only. And that's because investors are trying to maximize the tax benefits that they've been able to generate.

headline: Removal of negative gearing on existing properties expected to materially reduce investor demand in Australian housing
reasoning: Daniel Yu highlighted that recent tax changes removing negative gearing benefits on existing properties are expected to cause a significant drop-off in the investor segment of housing demand. Investors have historically accounted for around 41% of total home lending volumes. While owner-occupiers could theoretically replace some investor demand, sentiment is weak and many are waiting on the sidelines to see how far prices fall. A shift from investor to owner-occupier loans also hurts bank margins because investor loans carry higher interest rates.
quote: Amongst the buyers, you know, we probably would see a bigger drop off in the the investor segment. Given the recent tax changes to remove negative gearing on existing properties. Um, so I guess in theory, if there are less buyers turning up at auctions and so forth, you know, they could technically be replaced by an unoccupied. But as I just mentioned, I think sentiment is pretty weak. So you are going to see a lot of owner occupiers, you know, waiting on the sidelines, waiting just to see how far, um, property prices may fall.

headline: Cuts Australian GDP growth forecast materially, citing higher rates and housing market weakness
reasoning: Moody's reduced its Australian GDP growth forecast by 40 basis points to 1.9% for the current year and by 70 basis points to 1.6% for the following year. The combination of higher interest rates and slower growth is expected to increase non-performing loans across the banking system. Falling house prices reduce household sentiment and spending, with flow-on effects to businesses. However, Moody's sees unemployment staying below 5% as a key mitigant, alongside borrower repayment buffers and bank loan-to-value ratios averaging below 50%.
